item.title: New York state reports first measles-linked child death in over 30 years amid outbreak
item.description: The New York State Department of Health said on Monday that a child in Lewis County had died in connection with an ongoing measles outbreak, marking the state's first known measles-associated death in more than 30 years. Last month, Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in response to the measles outbreak across areas of New York and neighboring states. "The Department has offered resources to Lewis County to assist with community outreach and support local vaccination efforts — both in response to this case, and as part of our ongoing efforts to support counties that are facing this ongoing measles outbreak," the state department said. The death comes as the U.S. experiences its worst measles resurgence in decades. Hochul told Reuters in October that the state would seek federal assistance to help contain the outbreak, but did not confirm whether it had submitted a formal request for a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention Epidemic Intelligence Service, or Epi-Aid, response. item.title: [COVER STORY] President, first lady to get new passports after personal data exposure
item.description: President Lee Jae Myung and first lady Kim Hea Kyung are having new passports issued after their passport and other personal information were leaked, the foreign ministry said, Tuesday. The government and the police are investigating how the data was exposed, although they believe it was a leak, not an external cyberattack. “The foreign ministry is swiftly taking measures to ensure the smooth reissuance of passports for all affected individuals, including the president and first lady,” ministry spokesperson Park Doo-soon said during a briefing. The measures came after it was known that sensitive personal information of 168 people who were aboard the presidential jet for Lee’s trip to Europe in June had been uploaded on a security-related paid website. The leak affected not only the presidential couple but also ranking officials, including then-chief of staff for policy Kim Yong-beom, National Security Adviser Wi Sung-lac, current Prime Minister Han Seong-sook and several Cabinet members, as well as senior officials from Cheong Wa Dae and the foreign ministry, security personnel and

item.title: Trump admin asks top court to set aside 20,000 California ballots
item.description: WASHINGTON — The Trump administration asked the US Supreme Court on Monday to force California to set aside the mail-in ballots of more than 20,000 people it claims may not be American citizens. The move, one day ahead of crucial midterm elections, comes after lower courts last week -- and again on Monday -- rejected the demand by the Department of Justice (DOJ), with one judge calling it brazen pre-election "interference." Solicitor General D. John Sauer, in an emergency filing with the Supreme Court, said that "once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back." "The only way to preserve the district court's ability to grant relief to the United States after a full merits proceeding, therefore, is to segregate the challenged ballots now," Sauer said. The California ballot case appears to be another attempt by the administration to cast doubt on the results of Tuesday's vote, in which President Donald Trump's Republican Party is at risk of losing control of Congress. item.title: BOK sees consumer inflation remaining near 3% in November
item.description: Consumer prices are expected to rise into the high 2 percent range in November due to an upward trend in core inflation, the central bank said Tuesday. "Consumer prices rose at a slower pace in October as shipments of agricultural products improved, but prices of private services and durable goods remained elevated," Deputy Gov. Lee Ji-ho said during a meeting to review inflation trends. "In November, inflation is expected to remain in the high 2 percent range, affected by global oil prices and a continued upward trend in core inflation." Earlier in the day, government data showed that the country's consumer prices rose 2.8 percent last month from a year earlier, slowing from 2.9 percent in September and 3.1 percent in August. Prices of agricultural, livestock and fishery products fell 1.7 percent over the same period, while petroleum product prices advanced 14.9 percent on-year. Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, stood at 2.8 percent on-year in October. item.title: [TEST DRIVE] BYD Sealion 6 DM-i excels in quietness, range
item.description: Starting BYD Korea's Sealion 6 DM-i plug-in hybrid SUV, the first thing that stood out was the exceptional quietness of its cabin. Driving through city streets and along highways, the SUV felt more like a mid-size luxury sedan than a family-oriented SUV. In the name Sealion 6 DM-i, DM-i stands for “Dual Mode-intelligent,” BYD’s proprietary plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV) technology, which powers the vehicle's long-range drive. Its cabin remained remarkably quiet at low speeds, when the electric motor does most of the work. Minor vibrations were barely noticeable, while the suspension softened the impact of speed bumps and uneven pavement. The result was a relaxed, composed ride that made long-distance driving less tiring. On a roughly 100-kilometer round trip between Seoul and Paju, Gyeonggi Province, the SUV proved remarkably easy on the driver, with minimal fatigue and impressive fuel efficiency that exceeded expectations. The Sealion 6 DM-i is not built to deliver the explosive acceleration or sharp handling of a performance electric vehicle (EV). Its appeal lies elsewher

item.title: Police release identity of suspect in Seoul building arson
item.description: Police on Tuesday released the identity and mug shots of a suspect accused of setting fires at two patent firms in southern Seoul last month and leaving 26 people injured. The Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency posted the photos of Lee Myung-soo, 77, on its website following a decision by a review committee. Lee is suspected of committing arson in two buildings in Seoul's southern ward of Gangnam on Oct. 20, He was taken into custody shortly after the fires and was referred to the prosecution last week on charges of arson and attempted murder. Investigators believe the suspect planned the arson and was likely aware of people inside the offices. Lee has claimed that he was scammed by the patent firms and only wanted to scare people, not hurt them. Korea releases the identities and mug shots of those suspected of committing serious crimes when there is substantial evidence that they committed the offenses.

item.title: Foreigners' card spending in Seoul jumps nearly 58% to $6.57 bil.
item.description: Foreign visitors' card spending in Seoul jumped nearly 58 percent from a year earlier in the first nine months of 2026, driven by a record number of visitors, city government data showed Tuesday. Foreigners spent 8.84 trillion won ($6.57 billion) using credit and debit cards in Seoul from January to September, up 57.7 percent from the same period last year, according to the data. The figure has already surpassed the annual total of 7.94 trillion won for 2025. By sector, shopping accounted for the largest share at 46 percent, followed by medical and wellness services at 23.8 percent. Food and beverages took up 13.3 percent, while accommodation accounted for 10.4 percent. By district, Gangnam Ward led spending with 29.6 percent of the total, followed by Jung Ward at 27.7 percent and Mapo Ward at 7.1 percent. Spending expanded in most areas across the city, with foreigners' card spending more than doubling in the Gangdong, Guro, Dongdaemun and Seongdong wards. item.title: Seoul shares down over 2% late Tuesday morning on AI concerns
item.description: Korean stocks traded more than 2 percent lower late Tuesday morning, led by tech losses amid lingering woes about the excessive pace of artificial intelligence (AI) spending. Opening 2.46 percent lower, the benchmark Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) fell 145.02 points, or 2.48 percent, to 5,714.06 as of 11:20 a.m. Overnight on Wall Street, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite and the S&P 500 closed 1.07 percent and 0.51 percent lower, respectively, ahead of the U.S. midterm elections slated for Tuesday. Investor sentiment was dampened by concerns that massive spending on AI infrastructure is undermining tech firms' near-term profitability. In Seoul, tech shares led the decline. Market bellwether Samsung Electronics sank 2.95 percent, and its chipmaking rival SK hynix slid 3.8 percent. Hanmi Semiconductor, a leading chip equipment maker, fell 4.17 percent, and SK Square, the parent of SK hynix, tumbled 4 percent. Steel giant POSCO Holdings slumped 5.3 percent, and leading oil refinery SK Innovation plunged 7.76 percent. The Korean won was trading at 1,341 won against the U.S. dollar as of

item.title: Russia bombs aid center and shelter in southern Ukraine, killing 26, officials say
item.description: KYIV, Ukraine — Russia bombed an aid distribution center and neighboring shelter in southern Ukraine on Monday, killing 26 people, Ukrainian officials said. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X that strikes first targeted a school building used to distribute humanitarian aid and then took aim at a nearby shelter. “This is further proof that Russia wants no de-escalation,” Zelenskyy said. The attacks in the village of Komyshuvakha, in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, occurred as a limited ceasefire expired Monday in Kherson, a different region in the country's south. The limited ceasefire agreement had allowed humanitarian aid and evacuation missions into front-line areas in Russian-occupied territory. “There was a moment when the next steps could have shown that progress toward peace was possible,” Zelenskyy said. “With these killings, Russia is sending an entirely opposite signal: Russia is counting on more killings.” Zelenskyy later said in an address to the nation that Ukraine was expecting Russia to escalate its attacks at a time when the country

item.title: BTS concerts in Taiwan, Indonesia to be screened at movie theaters in over 80 countries
item.description: Two shows from K-pop supergroup BTS' upcoming tour in Taiwan and Jakarta will be livestreamed at movie theaters in more than 80 countries and regions, the group's agency said Tuesday. The live viewings will feature the group's second-day show in Kaohsiung, Taiwan, on Nov. 21 and its third-day show in Jakarta, Indonesia, on Dec. 29, BigHit Music said in a notice posted on K-pop fan community platform Weverse. The Kaohsiung and Jakarta concerts will be shown on about 3,300 and 2,800 large screens worldwide, respectively. In South Korea, audiences can watch them at three major cinema chains — CGV, Lotte Cinema and Megabox. BigHit Music said screening times will be adjusted for different time zones, meaning viewers in some regions will watch delayed broadcasts one to two days later. The shows are part of the Asian leg of the group's "ARIRANG" tour, set to kick off in Kaohsiung on Nov. 19. The septet will hold a total of 15 performances across five cities that also include Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur and Singapore. item.title: Consumer prices up 2.8% in October, remain in 2% range for 2nd month
item.description: Korea's consumer prices rose 2.8 percent in October from a year earlier, data showed Tuesday, as agricultural product prices continued to decline despite energy costs remaining elevated. According to data from the Ministry of Data and Statistics, consumer price growth eased to 2.8 percent in October from 2.9 percent in September and 3.1 percent in August. The data ministry said petroleum products' prices advanced 14.9 percent year-on-year in October, contributing 0.56 percentage point to the month's year-on-year inflation rate. item.title: Far from the campaign trail, Trump promotes his Reflecting Pool makeover before Election Day
item.description: WASHINGTON — U.S. President Donald Trump stood silently Monday while triumphant music played as he held up a poster showing an image of the algae-clogged pool in front of the Lincoln Memorial. It was the final moment of his last big speech before Election Day, far away from the campaign trail where Republicans were trying to make their case to voters to hang onto control of Congress. The president's decision to spend the day before the pivotal midterms showing off his renovations in the nation's capital instead of barnstorming around the country was a puzzling way to pitch America on keeping his party in power. “It starts just with the setting being bizarre and being very self-focused,” said Doug Heye, a Republican strategist. “And then you had the pictures and the posters on the easels and all of that — none of which help a single undecided voter in the last day of the elections move to the Republican Party.” Heye, a former communications director at the Republican National Committee, said Trump’s Reflecting Pool speech was the “last thing” Republican candidates needed

item.title: Glass Lewis supports Lee Jae-keun's appointment as KB Financial chairman
item.description: Glass Lewis has advised shareholders to support the appointment of Lee Jae-keun as chairman of KB Financial Group, according to a voting recommendations report exclusively obtained by The Korea Times on Tuesday. The world’s second-largest proxy advisory firm said it had identified “no substantial issues for shareholder concern” regarding the proposed appointment. The report also flagged several ongoing issues facing the group, including allegations of collusion over loan terms and subsequent investigations by the Fair Trade Commission, as well as the Financial Supervisory Service’s investigation into the potential mis-selling of Hong Kong-linked equity-linked securities. While noting it had found no clear evidence linking the board to these matters that would warrant specific action at the upcoming shareholders’ meeting, Glass Lewis added that the ongoing legal proceedings and discussions would continue to be monitored. item.title: Korea prepares launch of new SMR review system this month: nuclear watchdog chief
item.description: Small modular reactors (SMRs) have emerged as an important, carbon-free energy source in the era of artificial intelligence (AI), where the explosive growth of data centers requires an unprecedented amount of stable power. In response to such shifts in energy demands, Korea is set to introduce a preliminary review system designed to streamline the commercial development and deployment of SMRs starting later this month. The system will allow SMR developers to undergo safety and design verifications before formal licensing. It has already been adopted in countries such as the United States and Canada. With less than a month to go ahead of the system's launch, around ten companies — both from home and abroad — have expressed their intent to apply, with some considering making a submission immediately after the system takes effect, the head of the country's nuclear watchdog said. item.title: N. Korea tests 'dispersal warhead' for cruise missiles following cluster bomb test
item.description: North Korea has tested a "dispersal warhead" for a strategic cruise missile, state media reported Tuesday, following its recent test of a cluster bomb for ballistic missiles. The Missile Administration conducted the tests Monday to assess the power of such a warhead and the missile's "vertical strike" capability, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). "The Warhead Institute of the Missile Administration said it confirmed that the middle-sized dispersal warhead tipped on the cruise missile is capable of turning into ashes a target area of 5 to 6 hectares with its highest-density power," it said. The Cruise Missile System Institute said it perfected the missile's vertical strike capability by improving its terminal maneuverability, adjusted for the targeted area's natural and geographical characteristics. "The necessity of developing a variety of weapon systems is urgent than ever before. item.title: US trade commission terminates Samsung chip patent probe following settlement with Netlist
item.description: WASHINGTON — The U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) has formally terminated a patent infringement investigation involving Samsung Electronics Co. and several major American technology companies following a settlement between the Korean chipmaker and U.S. chip firm Netlist Inc., according to a federal notice published Monday. The investigation centered on certain dynamic random access memory (DRAM) devices, products containing them and related components, according to the USITC notice published in the U.S. Federal Register. The case was launched in July following a complaint from Netlist, which alleged that certain memory products infringed its patents. Other companies named as respondents in the case included Google, Nvidia Corp., Broadcom Inc. and Super Micro Computer Inc. item.description: WASHINGTON — The White House on Monday highlighted U.S. President Donald Trump's trade agreement with Korea and a Alaska natural gas project involving Seoul among his fulfilled campaign promises, as it touted his achievements on the eve of the U.S. midterm elections. item.title: N. Korean leader's sister blasts FBI's crypto theft probe as 'political provocation'
item.description: North Korea on Tuesday flatly dismissed the outcome of a U.S. investigation that blamed Pyongyang for a massive cryptocurrency theft from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, calling it a "grave political provocation" against the North. Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, made the remarks, referring to the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation's (FBI) announcement Saturday that the regime is responsible for the theft of more than US$6 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance. The FBI linked the theft to a North Korean hacking group it calls TraderTraitor, a name previously tied to other cryptocurrency heists. "The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cyber criminal state', claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident," Kim said in a statement carried by the North's official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). item.title: THE summit to explore turning university research into business in Seoul
item.description: The Times Higher Education (THE) Innovation & Impact Summit 2026 will take place at Korea University in Seoul from Nov. 17 to 19, bringing together global university leaders and industry experts to explore ways to turn academic research into commercially viable technologies and businesses. Under the theme "Universities, industry and investors: Connecting research with commercialisation," the three-day summit will examine strategies for strengthening cooperation between academia and industry, attracting investment and fostering innovation. The event comes as universities worldwide face growing pressure to demonstrate the economic and social impact of their research amid rapid advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and intensifying global competition for technological leadership. The event is expected to draw more than 300 participants from over 150 institutions and organizations worldwide, including university leaders, researchers, investors and industry experts. item.description: Nobody expected September and October to be this much fun, at least for K-pop. Over the same two months, one K-pop heavyweight confessed his belief that the genre had run its course, while another stormed back onto the scene with a shiny, wildly ambitious new project. That's K-pop for you — just when you think you know which way the ball is bouncing, it ricochets somewhere else entirely. In between, BLACKPINK members dropped solo singles back-to-back, three of the industry’s biggest names faced off on the same Monday, and a brand-new girl group topped Melon a day after its debut. item.title: A year after streamer crackdown, Bucheon's chaos eased but not gone
item.description: BUCHEON, Gyeonggi Province — Park Hye-ran, 47, a mother of a 6-year-old son, often finds it unsettling to walk around her neighborhood in Bucheon, Gyeonggi Province, a city known for its many online streaming creators airing outlandish broadcasts. “I’m worried about being filmed, and the broadcasting makes me uncomfortable. As early as the afternoon, many people are streaming around the food alley near Bucheon Station,” Park said, adding that it can’t be good for children to see. Last year, Bucheon made headlines for streamers who vied for viewer donations with attention-grabbing stunts such as dancing shirtless, singing loudly in public and mocking police officers called to the scene. Things turned violent when a YouTuber in her 30s was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after stabbing a man in his 30s with a weapon during his livestream. In response, the city announced a crackdown on streamers in September 2025, citing broadcasts that seriously damaged its brand image and harmed merchants and residents. It applied crime prevention strategies using environmental design

item.title: Trump forgoes traditional campaign trail stops in final push before Election Day
item.description: WASHINGTON — As Republicans and Democrats were making their final pitch to voters on the eve of Election Day, President Donald Trump opted to forgo the campaign trail and planned a speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, drawing attention to an expensive, problem-plagued repair job in a place far away from most of the people his party wants to persuade. It was an unusual place to make a closing argument for Republicans to keep control of Congress. But it conforms with the way the president has devoted considerable time, attention and money in his second term on beautifying his Washington surroundings. Democrats, for their part, were spending the last 24 hours before Election Day making their case in areas where Republicans have long dominated, while trying to contain the fallout from a messy intraparty split in Michigan. Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed was brushing aside concerns that his prospects could be hurt after his former primary opponent threw her support behind his Republican opponent Mike Rogers. item.title: Traditional music teachers exploited authority to sexually abuse students: Court records
item.description: Sex crimes in the traditional Korean music community persist, fueled by the enormous influence teachers wield over students’ future careers and the close-knit, insular nature of the industry. Following the Hankook Ilbo’s in-depth coverage of sexual exploitation in the traditional music scene, victims continued to come forward with accounts of widespread sexual harassment and assault. Court rulings also revealed disturbing details of the crimes. An analysis by the Hankook Ilbo of court rulings from 2010 to 2026 involving sexual offenses committed by traditional music instructors who abused their positions of authority over students found that seven of the 11 cases involved underage victims. In four of those cases, the victims were younger than 13. Cases involving adult victims also revealed how perpetrators exploited their control over students’ future careers to subject them to repeated abuse. Even as they suffered, victims found it difficult to speak out, and some eventually left the traditional music community altogether. The crimes typically took place in lesson rooms or class

item.title: Major automakers urge US Congress to pass permanent ban on Chinese vehicles
item.description: WASHINGTON — A group representing nearly all major automakers on Monday urged U.S. lawmakers to pass a permanent ban on Chinese vehicles when they return next week for a quick session after the midterm congressional elections. In September, the Senate sponsors of the bipartisan effort to ban Chinese vehicles agreed to delay an effort to fast-track the bill until November despite overwhelming support. "We need to protect the U.S. market from a flood of Chinese imports that carry surveillance risk and disadvantage current manufacturers that have made generational investments in American communities," said John Bozzella, who heads the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, which represents General Motors, Toyota, Volkswagen and other major automakers. Some congressional aides and auto lobbyists think if Democrats win control of Congress there may not be enough time to approve the Chinese vehicle ban before this session ends in December. item.title: How US news organizations will make midterm race calls
item.description: On Tuesday night, newsrooms across the U.S. will call winners in one of the country's most closely contested midterm election cycles in recent years, long before all the votes are counted. Most television networks and digital outlets rely on two providers for vote counts: the Associated Press or election-data firm Decision Desk HQ. Some news outlets such as the Wall Street Journal and MS NOW will rely on the AP for race calls, while others like Fox News and CBS News will make their own projections based on the AP vote count, exit polls, early-vote totals and their own statistical modeling. The first calls will start soon after polls begin to close in the United States, first with Indiana and Kentucky at 6 p.m. ET (2300 GMT), and shortly after in Georgia, South Carolina, Vermont and Virginia at 7 p.m. (0000 GMT on November 4). In certain races there may be an instant call if much of the voting has already taken place. Low public trust complicates race calls for news outlets. While more than 60 percent of Americans have some confidence in news organizations to report accurate election resu

item.title: Caught cold: fridge cyberattack highlights internet gadget weaknesses
item.description: PARIS — Cyberattacks affecting supermarket refrigeration systems in several European countries on Monday highlighted the risks associated with connecting industrial equipment to the internet. After a previous attack in France in October, several chains in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden experienced stark rises in fridge and freezer temperatures on Monday, forcing them to throw away spoilt produce. Real world effects Industrial equipment such as refrigeration systems, once operated largely offline, is now commonly connected to the internet so it can be monitored and managed remotely, cybersecurity specialists including Antoine Hautin, secretary-general of the Almond cybersecurity consultancy, told AFP. That connectivity can also provide an avenue for attackers to interfere with physical systems through digital networks. In France, the attackers targeted the fridge regulation system made by the Danish firm Danfoss, which is used by many shops. "Most of the time, that's done through a web interface. item.title: Unwanted ballots worry Korean green card holders amid US voting crackdown
item.description: SEATTLE — With the Trump administration stepping up its crackdown on noncitizen voting ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections, some Korean green card holders are worried that receiving election ballots they never requested could land them in immigration trouble. Across online forums and social media discussions, including Korean American communities, legal residents have shared accounts of receiving ballots or voter-registration materials despite not being U.S. citizens. "I'm a green card holder, but ballots come to my house every time," one user wrote. Another said she and her husband, both lawful permanent residents, had received jury summonses, and that her husband had also received election-related mail. item.description: NEW YORK — The U.S. stock market is rising Monday and recovering some of last week's sell-off that was led by the tech and AI industries. The S&P 500 climbed 0.3 percent, coming off its third straight losing week, and pulled within 2.8 percent of its all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 494 points, or 1 percent, as of 12:50 p.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 0.4 percent higher. Stocks got a lift from sharp drops for oil prices, which headed back down in their latest yo-yo move on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global industry to return to normal. The price for a barrel of Brent crude, the international standard, fell 7.5 percent to $104.92. The price for the most actively traded contract in the Brent market has been veering between roughly $70 and $120 per barrel since just before the war began, and it’s been quick to reverse direction. item.title: Trump asks Supreme Court to sideline 20,000 California mail ballots
item.description: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump's administration appealed to the Supreme Court on Monday in its push to sideline thousands of disputed California mail ballots the day before the pivotal midterm elections. The emergency appeal came after an appeals court rejected the request to set aside some 20,000 ballots from people the federal government suspects may not be citizens. The federal government says those ballots should not be counted until the voters’ status can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens. The Republican Trump administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite them being rare. A district court judge forcefully denied the Justice Department's request and warned that the demand could disenfranchise citizens in the Nov. 3 midterm elections to determine control of Congress. item.title: Iran says in 'intensive' negotiations with US to avert war
item.description: TEHRAN — Iran on Monday said "intensive" exchanges were underway with Washington and offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz under strict conditions, as efforts escalated to avert a return to war. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said indirect talks were taking place via mediators. China also urged a return to negotiations, while Iran's security chief discussed the conflict with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Oil prices, sent rocketing by Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz energy corridor, dropped more than six percent on Monday on optimism over the eight-month-old conflict. "Given the sensitivity and gravity of the current situation, consultations and deliberations are very intensive," Araghchi said in a video interview with the official IRNA news agency. item.title: Binance clients pull $4.7 billion after hack as crypto world studies fallout
item.description: SINGAPORE/PARIS — Binance's customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest financial heist in history. The exchange froze withdrawals for about 48 hours after the hack, which which the FBI said was carried out by North Korea, then started allowing customers to withdraw again on Sunday morning. The theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact on Binance, which has vowed to repay customers in full, and on the wider market. Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3% of assets on the platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up. The majority of the withdrawals from the platform were in the form of Tether's USDT stablecoin, Binance added. The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle's USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. Binance itself proce

item.title: New cyberattack on supermarket fridges sweeps across Europe
item.description: STOCKHOLM/BRUSSELS/LONDON — A hacking attack on European supermarkets spread across the continent on Monday, hitting fridges and freezers from Sweden to Belgium and forcing stores to throw away food in an incident that echoed a similar attack in France last month. The attack, which raised temperatures in refrigerator and freezer units at dozens of stores, hit supermarket groups Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt in Belgium and Luxembourg, as well as Swedish grocers ICA and Coop. Furniture-to-meatballs retailer IKEA also saw at least one store affected. "Everything is destroyed," Engla Ingwall, sales manager at an ICA franchise store in Stockholm, told Reuters during a visit to the store on Monday, adding the attack occurred at 2 a.m. (0100 GMT) but was only noticed hours later. "There has been a cyberattack and all our freezers reached 50 degrees (Celsius)." A spokesperson for privately held ICA said the company was aware that a "limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems". According to KBS, the personal information of 168 people, including Lee, staff from Cheong Wa Dae and the foreign ministry, along with reporters covering the presidential office, was posted on a website in a file titled "List of passengers (Republic of Korea-Belgium)." The Republic of Korea is the official name of South Korea. The list appeared related to passengers who traveled aboard the presidential plane during Lee's trip to Belgium, Italy and France in June. KBS reported that the file was available for download and was even posted on June 2 ahead of Lee's trip. The information included Korean and English names, affiliations, positions, dates of birth, passport numbers and their expiration dates. item.title: Latino Voters Swing Away from Trump for "Terrorizing Our Communities": Marisa Franco of Mijente
item.description:
In 2024, Donald Trump won the presidency with the support of 44% of Hispanic voters, suggesting that a major realignment in party preferences might be underway. But just two years later, it appears much of that support has eroded. Sixty-one percent of Hispanic voters say they will now support Democrats in the midterms, including 11% who previously had voted for President Trump.

We get a bird’s-eye view of what to expect from the Latino vote from Marisa Franco, the co-founder and director of the advocacy organization Mijente. While ICE brutality will be at the front of voters’ minds, she says, Democrats cannot continue to take Latino voters for granted. “The vast majority of Latinos are working-class. Quite simply, they voted for Trump because they were looking at issues of economy, cost, inflation,” explains Franco. “And at the end of the day, these same issues have worsened under Trump’s administration, under Republican control. So people, I think, are looking for someone who’s going to explain what’s happening and propose solutions and be dogged about finding them.”

item.title: Democratic Socialists on the Rise: Darializa Avila Chevalier & Claire Valdez Set to Win House Seats
item.description:
New York City is preparing to send two DSA members, presumptive election night winners Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, to Capitol Hill. DSA-backed candidates made historic gains in this year’s Democratic primaries, with at least five expected to join current DSA members Rashida Tlaib and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in the House. But can socialism really make headway in the halls of Congress? Democracy Now! fellows Amba Guerguerian and Diego Ramos report.

“Our task is going to be winning our colleagues over to our position and finding common ground,” Valdez tells Democracy Now! “Some of the most popular policies in our country’s history have been socialist policies,” says Avila Chevalier. “They have been the things that working people have organized for and won.”

item.title: Election Protection: NAACP on Voter Suppression & Deployment of Federal Poll Monitors
item.description:
As President Donald Trump continues to cast doubt on the integrity of U.S. elections, signaling his intentions to challenge results unfavorable to Republicans, we go to Washington, D.C., where a federal judge ruled Monday night that the Department of Justice can deploy election monitors to polling sites across the country, as long as they are not law enforcement officers with the power to make arrests. “In some respects, this is a victory for voters. Every voter in our country deserves to be able to cast a ballot today, free from intimidation,” says Kristen Clarke of the NAACP, which sued to challenge the DOJ’s plans to deploy ICE agents and other armed officers to the polls.

The NAACP was also part of a coalition that intervened when the Trump administration attempted to force California to set aside about 20,000 mail-in ballots that it alleged were sent incorrectly to noncitizens. “This was a baseless, error-prone, shoddy 11th-hour attempt to hijack the election in California, plain and simple, and it’s now been rejected by four courts,” Clarke says. The administration’s attacks on voters “are not bearing fruit,” she adds. “We anticipate and are ready for anything that they may throw our way.”

item.title: "Democracy Itself Is on the Ballot": Voters Weigh 150+ Ballot Initiatives, from Wealth Tax to Abortion
item.description: As voters in the United States head to the polls, we take a look at what’s on the ballot with Chris Melody Fields Figueredo of the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center. “This is a consequential election, and voters are going to be able to vote on democracy itself, whether they can participate in elections, how congressional districts are drawn, whether they will have autonomy of their own bodies,” says Fields Figueredo, who previews some of the over 145 ballot initiatives being considered across the country, including California’s billionaire wealth tax and measures concerning reproductive, voting and LGBTQ+ rights.

item.title: Japan launches new national agency to deal with disasters
item.description: TOKYO — Japan on Monday launched a new national agency focused on disaster management to improve the country's preparedness if there's a megaquake along the Pacific coast or in Tokyo, or an eruption of Mount Fuji. More than 350 workers at the National Disaster Management Agency will oversee preparedness, emergency response and reconstruction efforts. The agency was not created in anticipation of any specific calamity, but to address concerns about whether the nation is prepared for a crisis on the scale of the 2011 quake and tsunami in northern Japan, which killed nearly 20,000 people, and the subsequent Fukushima nuclear disaster. Japan, which lies along the Pacific "Ring of Fire,” is one of the most disaster-prone countries but it has never had an agency dedicated to the task. “As the command center of disaster response, we will do everything to strengthen our preparedness to protect people's lives and properties ... and aim to become the world's most prepared,” Reconstruction Minister Goshi Hosono said. He will manage the agency headed by Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi

item.title: Top court upholds antitrust watchdog's $13.8 mil. fine on Broadcom
item.description: Korea's top court has upheld the country's antitrust watchdog's decision to impose an 18.6 billion won ($13.8 million) fine on U.S. chipmaker Broadcom Inc. for unfair business practices against Samsung Electronics, sources said Monday. According to the sources, the Supreme Court on Tuesday upheld a lower court ruling against Broadcom in a lawsuit the U.S. company filed against the Fair Trade Commission (FTC). In 2023, the FTC fined Broadcom for using its superior position to force Samsung to sign a long-term agreement in 2020. According to the watchdog, Broadcom compelled Samsung to purchase at least $760 million worth of its smartphone parts annually from 2021 to 2023 and required the South Korean tech giant to compensate for any shortfall if its purchases fell below that amount. Broadcom filed a lawsuit challenging the FTC's decision in November 2023. In May, however, the Seoul High Court ruled against Broadcom, finding the fine justified. An FTC decision, when challenged, is reviewed by the Seoul High Court, whose ruling can be appealed to the Supreme Court.

item.description: Korea and India held the inaugural meeting of their economic security dialogue in Seoul on Monday to discuss ways to maintain the momentum of their cooperation in stabilizing supply chains and advancing cooperation in advanced technologies, Seoul's presidential office said. Monday's meeting was held as a follow-up to the Korean and Indian leaders' summit in April, during which they agreed to launch the dialogue to enhance supply chain resilience and advance cooperation in cutting-edge technologies. Song Ki-ho, vice chief of Cheong Wa Dae's National Security Office, represented Korea at the dialogue, while India was represented by Pavan Kapoor, deputy national security adviser of India, according to the presidential office. item.title: Finance minister, Hyundai Motor chief discuss EV policies: sources
item.description: Korea's finance minister met with the head of Hyundai Motor Group to discuss ways to develop the country's electric vehicle (EV) industry, along with government tax incentives for the sector, sources said Monday. Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il met with Hyundai Motor Group Executive Chair Euisun Chung for around 20 minutes ahead of a roundtable held on the day at the company's research center in Hwaseong, south of Seoul, according to the sources. During the meeting, the two also exchanged views on applying tax cuts for EVs produced in the country, the sources said. item.title: KAI delivers first 2 FA-50 fighter jets to Malaysia
item.description: Korea Aerospace Industries Ltd. (KAI) said Monday it has delivered the first two FA-50 light combat aircraft to Malaysia under a 2023 contract to supply 18 jets to the Southeast Asian country. The two FA-50M aircraft departed from KAI's headquarters in Sacheon, about 300 kilometers southeast of Seoul, on Thursday and arrived at Malaysia's Kuantan Air Base on Sunday. The aircraft will be formally handed over to the Royal Malaysian Air Force after completing final acceptance tests. The delivery marks the first shipment under the 2023 deal, aimed at replacing Malaysia's aging Hawk 108 and 208 advanced trainer and light combat aircraft as part of the country's military modernization program.

item.title: Seoul Plaza to host night market Friday featuring 47 small businesses
item.description: Seoul Plaza will turn into an evening marketplace Friday, offering shoppers a chance to discover products from 47 small businesses, enjoy live performances and receive discounts as the city looks to bring more spending into the nighttime economy. The Seoul Metropolitan Government will hold its 2026 Small Business Day celebration from 10 a.m. to 9 p.m. Friday, extending operating hours by two hours from last year to accommodate office workers and other visitors unable to attend during the day. The event marks Small Business Day, observed annually on Nov. 5, and carries the theme "Better everyday lives created by small shops, Seoul as a city of quality living." Participating businesses will offer products ranging from meal kits, premium teas and baked goods to handmade soaps, accessories, leather goods and traditional crafts. item.title: RIIZE turns to literature to deepen story behind 'Insomnia'
item.description: K-pop group RIIZE is turning to literature to tell a deeper story, pairing its new single "Insomnia" with fiction and illustration in an experiment that puts emotion and storytelling ahead of performance. The six-member group released "Insomnia" on Oct. 26, offering an acoustic pop track steeped in the mood of a chilly autumn night. The song marks a departure from the dynamic sound and performance-driven presentation often associated with RIIZE, bringing the members' vocals to the forefront instead. Its lyrics explore thoughts of another person that become increasingly vivid as the night deepens, along with the complicated emotions that grow from them. Against the backdrop of a sleepless night, the members sing about a more complex and introspective emotional state. The shift extends to the music video. Rather than centering on choreography, it adopts a dramatized, cinematic format in which each member experiences insomnia and emotional distress in a different way following a particular incident. item.title: Seoul names 19 'medical-friendly' hotels for foreign patients
item.description: Seoul has designated 19 hotels and accommodations as “medical-friendly” lodgings tailored for international patients and their families, part of an effort to capture a growing global market traveling to Korea for health care, the city government said Monday. According to the Korea Health Industry Development Institute, about 1.76 million foreign patients were treated at medical institutions in Seoul in 2025, a record high. That is 3.7 times the roughly 470,000 in 2023. Seoul accounted for 87.2 percent of the roughly 2.01 million foreign patients treated nationwide last year. The Seoul Metropolitan Government and the Seoul Tourism Organization chose the 19 facilities from 40 applicants in the program’s first year. The selection involved document reviews, on-site inspections and expert evaluations. Unlike regular tourists, foreign patients often need long stays that follow their treatment schedules, rooms for family members or caregivers, and places to recover after surgery or other procedures. item.title: Busan Fireworks Festival to light up Gwangalli Beach Saturday
item.description: Korea’s southern port city of Busan will host its massive annual fireworks display Saturday along Gwangalli Beach, illuminating the landmark Gwangan Bridge across the bay, city officials said Monday. The hourlong show starts at 7 p.m. Fireworks will be launched from three spots, Gwangalli Beach, Igidae Park and Dongbaek Island, to give the show more depth. The program will open with a 15-minute show by China’s Sunny Fireworks. It will be followed by a 30-minute show by Korea’s Hanwha Corp. on the theme “Busan’s dream,” featuring 25-inch shells, waterfall-style “Niagara” fireworks and multimedia lighting on the bridge. A five-minute “curtain call” display will then offer thanks citizens and festival staff. Before the fireworks show, the Black Eagles, the Korean Air Force’s aerobatic team, will put on an air show at 4 p.m., alongside beach events and busking by local indie bands. The city will offer some 17,000 paid seats. About 3,000 more seats than last year have been added, all set aside for foreign tourists and sold through overseas travel agencies and online trav

item.description: Visitors to Unhyeon Palace in central Seoul can step into the shoes of 19th-century royal investigators this month, searching for secret clues across moonlit courtyards to solve a fictional mystery involving a stolen royal seal. The Seoul Metropolitan Government will host "Moonlit Secret Mission: Find the Missing Royal Seal" on select evenings from Wednesday to Nov. 29. The interactive program transforms the historic royal residence located in Seoul's central Jongno District into an immersive stage for storytelling, puzzle-solving and traditional Korean arts. Participants play secret agents recruited by the father, navigating the palace grounds at dusk to question historical characters, solve riddles and gather evidence. The two-hour program guides small groups through three key areas of the palace complex. item.title: LS Cable, LS Marine Solution sign deal on Taean offshore wind cable project
item.description: LS Cable & System and its affiliate LS Marine Solution have signed a deal with the developer of a 504-megawatt offshore wind farm off Korea’s west coast to supply and install its subsea cables, the companies said Monday. The two companies signed a capacity reservation agreement (CRA) with Taean Wind Power. A CRA reserves cable production capacity and installation vessel schedules before a final contract is signed. The agreement follows the developer’s selection of the two companies as preferred bidders in 2024. They are now reviewing cable specifications and the scope of installation work through engineering and site surveys. They plan to agree on the contract value and other details and sign a final contract within the year. The Taean offshore wind project is being jointly developed by state-run Korea Western Power, Singapore-based renewable energy company Vena Energy and Danish renewable energy investor Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners. item.title: KOSPI rallies over 2% as investors look past US tech rout
item.description: KOSPI rose more than 2 percent Monday, as institutional buying helped stocks rebound from early losses, shrugging off lingering concerns over the profitability of artificial intelligence (AI) investments. The benchmark closed at 5,859.08, up 2.24 percent. It opened 1.62 percent lower before reversing course as institutional investors stepped up purchases. Institutional investors bought a net 1.36 trillion won ($1.01 billion) of shares, while foreign and retail investors net sold 43.09 billion won and 1.41 trillion won, respectively. SK hynix gained 3.81 percent to close at 1,472,000 won, while Samsung Electronics climbed 1.78 percent to 229,000 won. SK Square, which announced plans to return at least 4.3 trillion won to shareholders out of more than 6.2 trillion won expected from SK hynix's cash dividends, also gained 5.91 percent to close at 950,000 won. item.title: HYBE data breach exposes employee medical records, financial details
item.description: HYBE, the music agency behind K-pop group BTS, disclosed a cyberattack that exposed personal information of current and former employees and business partners, including resident registration numbers, credit card numbers and medical records. In an apology posted on its website, Oct. 18, the company said an internal security inspection detected unauthorized access through an outside vendor’s document preview software linked to its electronic approval system. Further investigation found similar access to its expense management system. According to the apology, the breaches occurred Sept. 12-13 and Oct. 3-5. Compromised information also included passport numbers, bank account details, addresses and phone numbers. The company did not disclose how many people were affected. “We deeply apologize for the concern caused by the personal information leak,” HYBE said in the notice. item.title: GS E&C data breach exposes blind spots in Korea's smart apartments
item.description: When Park, a 56-year-old homemaker living in an apartment complex in Suwon, Gyeonggi Province, heard that GS Engineering & Construction (GS E&C) had recently detected unauthorized access to a system containing residents’ personal information, the news struck a nerve. “Sure, I’ve had my personal information exposed in the Coupang and SK Telecom data breaches, among many others. Over time, I found myself becoming less concerned. Everyone seemed to be getting hit, and it felt like I was just another number in a database,” she said. This time, however, it felt much closer to home, quite literally. “The information involved could reveal details about my own household. Our apartment complex, like many newer developments, relies on smart home services for everyday tasks. item.title: Kia's Oct. sales rise 10% on strong SUV demand
item.description: Kia said Monday its vehicle sales rose 10.3 percent from a year earlier in October, driven by strong overseas demand for its sport utility vehicle (SUV) models. Kia sold a total of 291,219 vehicles last month, up from 264,017 units a year earlier, the company said in a press release. The figure includes sales of military vehicles. Robust demand for the Sportage, Sorento and Seltos SUVs boosted the monthly sales, the carmaker said. Domestic sales rose 27.5 percent on-year to 51,007 units, while overseas sales climbed 7.2 percent to 239,308 units, it said. Military vehicle sales gained 12.9 percent on-year to 904 units. Looking ahead, Kia said it will seek to maintain sales growth in the fourth quarter by launching gasoline-hybrid models in the United States and electrified cars in Europe.

item.title: Household loans again rise in Oct. despite tightened rules, higher rates
item.description: Household loans by major banks again rebounded in October from a month earlier despite tight borrowing regulations and higher rates, data showed Monday. Outstanding household loans at five major lenders — KB Kookmin Bank, Shinhan Bank, Hana Bank, Woori Bank and NH Nonghyup Bank — stood at 783.6 trillion won ($584 billion) as of end-October, up 2.77 trillion won from the previous month, according to data compiled by the banks. The rebound came a month after such loans fell for the first time in six months. The rise in household loans by banks was mainly attributed to a rise in both mortgage and credit loans. Mortgage loans rose for the seventh consecutive month in October, gaining 1.7 trillion won to 623.99 trillion won at the end of last month, according to the data. Credit loans also advanced 669 billion won to 108.89 trillion won over the cited period, following the previous month's 1.34 trillion-won fall. item.title: S. Korea officially recognizes 3 fishing crewmen abducted by N. Korea in 1973
item.description: South Korea has officially recognized three fishing crewmen abducted by North Korea decades ago, Seoul's unification ministry said Monday, bringing the total number of government-recognized abductees since the end of the 1950-53 Korean War to 519. The ministry added Jo Gi-won, Kim Yang-hun and Kim Dong-ho, who were forcibly taken to the North while aboard their fishing boat, the Daeyeong, near the South Korean border island of Yeonpyeong in 1973, to the list of post-war abductees eligible for "consolation" payments under a relevant law. It decided to provide 81 million won ($60,290) in consolation money to Jo's family members, while it is seeking to find the family members of the other abductees. The Daeyeong had not been counted among the boats whose sailors were abducted by the North until Kim Byeong-do, one of its crewmembers, returned to South Korea in 2003, according to an association of post-war abductees' family members. item.description: WASHINGTON — Democrats teed up final get-out-the-vote rallies Monday on the eve of midterm elections where they expect to win at least partial control of Congress and impose political constraints on President Donald Trump for the first time in two years. Rallies -- including by star Democratic Senate candidates James Talarico in Texas and Adam Hamilton in Kansas -- were capping a campaign of breathtaking tension and bitterness. For his closing argument, Trump chose a speech in Washington at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool -- a landmark that has become synonymous with the 80-year-old president's obsessive, controversial drive to redevelop the US capital. "We're going to win," he said on Sunday. Polls, however, show that Democrats are near certain to take the majority from Republicans in the House of Representatives and have a real shot at winning the currently Republican Senate. item.title: Korea's beloved actors leave behind generations of viewers
item.description: Korea’s most beloved veteran actors are leaving behind a deep sense of loss among audiences who grew up watching them on television and in movie theaters. The deaths of Lee Soon-jae, Ahn Sung-ki and Choi Bool-am within less than a year have marked the loss of three towering figures who helped shape Korea’s popular culture for decades. Each made a different contribution to the entertainment industry, but all became household names whose presence extended far beyond their performances. In Korea, they are often called “the nation’s favorite actors,” a term reserved for performers who have earned the affection and respect of generations of audiences. Their popularity went beyond fame. Through the characters they portrayed and the stories they brought into Korean homes, they became familiar companions in the everyday lives of millions. item.title: Korea, IMF to hold annual consultation on economy, financial policy
item.description: Korea will hold an annual consultation session with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) this week to discuss the country's overall economic situation and policies, the finance ministry said Monday. An IMF delegation, led by mission chief Corinne Delechat, is scheduled to have meetings with government ministries, including the finance, budget and industry ministries, the Bank of Korea (BOK) and other public and private institutions, according to the Ministry of Finance and Economy. The IMF team plans to hold a press conference on Nov. 17 to explain the results of the annual session after a separate meeting with Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il, it added. The IMF earlier revised up its growth forecast for Korea's economy to 3.3 percent for this year by 0.7 percentage point from its July projection amid the global semiconductor supercycle.

item.title: DL E&C to build 727-unit apartment complex in Naepo New Town
item.description: DL E&C is set to build a 727-unit apartment complex in Naepo New Town, a planned administrative city in South Chungcheong Province, amid ongoing development of the area's residential, educational and industrial infrastructure. The project, named e-Pyeonhansesang Naepo Edu Platz, will comprise nine buildings, rising up to 25 floors above two basement levels, with units ranging from 84 to 119 square meters. Of the total units, 605 will be 84-square-meter apartments offered through a public-private housing program, while the remaining 122 will be privately sold 119-square-meter units. The complex, scheduled for occupancy in August 2028, is located near the center of Naepo New Town, with elementary, middle and high schools within walking distance. Nearby amenities include the town's central commercial district, medical facilities, banks and government offices, including the South Chungcheong provincial government, police station and education office. item.description: The chief of Samsung Electro-Mechanics on Monday highlighted business opportunities in the artificial intelligence (AI) era, saying the market has significant room for growth as the industry expands. "The current AI industry is just January 1," Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Chang Duck-hyun said at a ceremony marking the 53rd anniversary of the company's founding, suggesting that the industry remains in its earliest stages despite concerns over its long-term profitability. item.title: Finance minister discusses economic ties, cooperation with US ambassador
item.description: Finance Minister Lee Hyoung-il met with U.S. Ambassador to Korea Michelle Steel on Monday to discuss ways to strengthen bilateral economic cooperation, the finance ministry said. During the meeting held at the government complex in Seoul, Lee said the Korea-U.S. alliance has expanded beyond security to encompass economic areas, including advanced industries, energy and supply chains, over the past 70 years, according to the Ministry of Finance and Economy. He expressed hope that Steel, who was born in Seoul, would help build bridges between the two countries and expand bilateral economic cooperation, drawing on her deep understanding of both countries. Lee also asked Steel to play a role in enhancing communication to resolve bilateral trade issues. The two sides shared the view that the allies should expand economic cooperation in a way that further strengthens the Seoul-Washington alliance, the ministry added.

item.description: Daewoo Engineering & Construction (E&C) said Monday it has asked the government to mediate a dispute with Korea's state-run nuclear power operator over a major nuclear reactor project in the Czech Republic. The company, which leads a construction consortium for the project, made the request to the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources after receiving formal notice Friday that Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) Co. had ended contract negotiations. "We have requested the ministry's mediation to resume contract negotiations and normalize the project as soon as possible," Daewoo E&C said in a statement. The Dukovany project, valued at about 25 trillion won ($17.5 billion), involves the construction of two 1,000-megawatt APR1000 nuclear reactors, a Korean-designed model, in the Czech Republic. item.title: Multicultural family benefits face review over 'fairness' concerns
item.description: The government and local authorities nationwide are launching a formal review of benefits for multicultural families after President Lee Jae Myung raised concerns that some programs unfairly disadvantage other households. The Ministry of Justice sent an official request to local governments late last month, asking them to provide details of their support policies for such families. item.title: Doubts on AI investment to test Korean economy
item.description: Growing concerns over the sustainability of the global artificial intelligence (AI) investment boom are translating into mounting financing pressures on major tech companies, raising fears that a slowdown in AI spending could deal an outsized blow to Korea's semiconductor-dependent economy. Tech giants such as Google, Meta and Amazon are heavily relying on debt to finance their massive capital expenditures, as borrowing costs continue to rise. This also adds pressure to the fundraising plans of AI developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic. This could eventually slow the pace of AI investment and weigh on memory chip prices, potentially sending shock waves through Korea's broader economy, which heavily relies on corporate tax revenue from Samsung Electronics and SK hynix. item.title: DPK welcomes Lee's budget speech; PPP slams failure to address N. Korea, economic woes
item.description: The ruling Democratic Party of Korea (DPK) on Monday welcomed President Lee Jae Myung's budget speech, while the main opposition People Power Party (PPP) criticized him for failing to address North Korea's threats and economic concerns. PPP lawmakers also staged a rally at the National Assembly ahead of Lee's speech on next year's budget proposal, condemning what they called a budget that disregards national debt and destroys the country's future. "President Lee came, said only what he wanted to say and left," PPP leader Jang Dong-hyeok wrote on Facebook. "He made no mention of real estate, the stock market or farmland, nor did he mention North Korea, the South Korea-U.S. alliance, public safety or judicial issues," Rep. Jang said. item.title: Samsung SDS breaks ground on AI data center in Gumi
item.description: Samsung SDS has begun construction of an artificial intelligence (AI) data center in Gumi, North Gyeongsang Province, marking the first step in Samsung Group's 60 trillion won ($44.6 billion) investment plan for the Yeongnam region. The company said Monday that the facility will be built on a 46,000-square-meter site in Gongdan-dong, with an initial power capacity of 60 megawatts, which can be expanded to 120 MW to meet growing demand for AI computing infrastructure. Construction began after Gumi City approved the project in late August, with completion targeted for the end of 2028. The project is part of Samsung's plan, announced in July, to turn the Yeongnam region into a global hub for physical AI innovation. The investment roadmap covers humanoid robots and AI data centers in Gumi, all-solid-state batteries in Ulsan, advanced packaging substrates and multilayer ceramic capacitors (MLCCs) for AI servers in Busan and high-value-added vessels in Geoje, South Gyeongsang Province. item.title: Discount subscriptions put money, personal data at risk, experts warn
item.description: Subscriptions to services such as Netflix and YouTube Premium cost an average of 65 percent less when bought through unofficial resellers, but buyers risk losing their accounts, their money and their personal data, a cybersecurity firm said Monday. Netherlands-based Surfshark compared official prices for 10 popular subscription services, including Netflix, Spotify, YouTube Premium and Duolingo, with prices on resale platforms. Resold subscriptions averaged about 6,200 won ($4.60) a month, compared with about 17,600 won through official channels. That is a saving of about 11,400 won a month, or more than 130,000 won a year. Resellers typically sell shared accounts or access to them, often at prices far below official rates. The study found that eight of the 10 services required a minimum 12-month commitment on resale platforms, and the other two required at least six months. Buyers who lose access before the term ends may have to rely on the reseller for help or a refund. Some platforms also asked for more personal information than needed. item.title: Major disaster could open door to N. Korea talks, Japanese disaster expert says
item.description: A major natural disaster in North Korea could create an opening for engagement with the isolated regime through humanitarian aid, according to a Japanese disaster expert who once coordinated with North Korean officials at the United Nations. He noted that the U.N. had discussed such an approach and that disasters have helped thaw relations elsewhere. “In the event of a major disaster in North Korea, neighboring countries — including China, South Korea, Russia and Japan — could potentially provide humanitarian assistance,” Yuichi Ono, professor at Tohoku University and deputy director of International Research Institute of Disaster Science (IRIDeS), said during a meeting with South Korean reporters visiting Japan as part of a South Korea-Japan journalists’ exchange program on Oct. 23, according to the joint press corps. item.title: Korea unveils $276 mil. 'Hangang' supercomputer
item.description: Korea has officially launched its sixth national supercomputer, named "Hangang" after the iconic Han River flowing through Seoul, to propel cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) and scientific research. The Ministry of Science and ICT and the state-run Korea Institute of Science and Technology Information (KISTI) marked the launch Monday at KISTI headquarters in Daejeon, the nation’s primary scientific and research hub located about 140 kilometers south of Seoul. The ceremony brought together roughly 200 leaders from across industry, academia and government research institutions. Constructed at a cost of 382.5 billion won ($276 million), Hangang replaces Nurion, the fifth-generation supercomputer deployed in 2018. Nurion ranked 11th globally at launch and supported 1,730 research projects over its eight-year lifespan. Those efforts produced 1,520 peer-reviewed papers, including 70 published in top-tier international journals such as Nature, Science and Cell. item.title: LG Electronics CEO eyes 'caregiving' as next frontier for AI-powered homes
item.description: The chief of LG Electronics said on Monday that "caregiving" could become the next frontier for artificial intelligence (AI)-powered services. In a post on his LinkedIn account, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Lyu Jae-cheol outlined the company's vision for AI-powered homes, saying they should go beyond simply adding AI features to connected devices. "This is the direction envisioned by LG Electronics' 'Zero-Labor Home' vision, which aims to free people from household chores," Lyu said. The Korean home appliance maker has been spearheading efforts to transform the way people manage their homes through its AI-powered appliance lineup, ranging from refrigerators to air purifiers. Rather than simply adding AI functions to connected devices, the goal should be to fundamentally change the way homes operate, he said. Lyu emphasized, however, that AI-powered homes should reduce the burden of repetitive household chores while leaving important decisions in the hands of users.

item.title: Retrial to begin next week for Uzbek national convicted of murder, robbery 16 years ago
item.description: A court will open a retrial next week for an Uzbek national who was sentenced to life in prison 16 years ago for killing and robbing a taxi driver in 2009, legal sources said Monday. According to the sources, the first hearing of the retrial for Bozorov Akmal, 37, will begin at 11 a.m. on Nov. 12 at the Changwon District Court in Changwon, about 300 kilometers southeast of Seoul. The Supreme Court finalized Akmal's life imprisonment in 2010 on charges of robbing and killing a 50-something taxi driver in Changwon in March 2009. After his first request for a retrial was rejected in 2015, he filed a second petition in January last year through Park Jun-young, a defense attorney known for handling retrial cases. Park pointed out numerous flaws in the original investigation, including forensic opinions on the victim's neck wounds, taxi routes, records from the National Forensic Service, phone logs and testimony regarding the weapon. item.title: Korean financial firms are buying into Japan's brokerage market
item.description: Japan's stock market rally and retail investing boom are attracting Korean financial firms seeking overseas growth, as mounting pressure on smaller brokerages creates acquisition opportunities, industry officials said Monday. Viva Republica, the operator of Korean fintech platform Toss, plans to acquire Cheer Securities through its Singapore-based subsidiary, Toss Global, in a deal valued at 4 billion yen ($25.35 million). It would mark Toss' first overseas acquisition. Cheer Securities, established in 2019 by Tokai Tokyo Financial Holdings, specializes in mobile trading, allowing customers to invest in stocks and exchange-traded funds in increments of 100 yen through its app. It also handles security token offerings. Mirae Asset Securities also signed an agreement Thursday to acquire Sanko Securities, a unit of Okasan Securities Group, through its U.S. subsidiary. Mirae Asset plans to inject 12 billion yen into its U.S. subsidiary, allocating about 5 billion yen toward the acquisition and the remainder to expanding its business in Japan after the transaction closes. item.title: Incheon airport's network fiasco raises questions over crisis readiness
item.description: Incheon International Airport’s latest check-in disruption has exposed its vulnerability to failures at external network providers, prompting calls for stronger contingency systems. The outage began around 4:30 a.m. Friday, when connectivity problems hit the global network of U.S.-based aviation communications provider ARINC, disrupting check-in operations at 13 airlines across both terminals. It delayed 38 flights and left around 1,200 passengers waiting at the airport, according to Incheon International Airport Corp. (IIAC). By the afternoon, ticketing operations at China Southern Airlines, China Eastern Airlines and Air China had nearly ground to a halt, forcing them to switch to manual procedures. The latest network fiasco clearly shows a structural vulnerability in airport operations. International airports and airlines rely on global IT providers to exchange passenger and reservation information, coordinate check-in procedures and issue boarding passes. Such platforms allow carriers to operate across multiple airports without building entirely separate systems at each location. Ho

Jang attended a preview exhibition for an Italian luxury jewelry brand at SONGEUN in Cheongdam-dong, southern Seoul, on Oct. 28. The dress's off-the-shoulder and backless silhouette accentuated Jang's shoulders and long, statuesque proportions, giving the K-pop star an almost Barbie-like appearance. She paired the dress with a delicate chain necklace that caught the light along her neckline and gold bangles on both wrists, adding a luxurious finish to the look. Black pointed-toe stiletto heels further elongated the silhouette, while Jang wore her hair in a high updo with loose strands framing her face for a polished yet soft finish. item.title: Experience ancient Korean commerce at Seoul's annual Yukuijeon Festival
item.description: Jongno, the historic heart of downtown Seoul, will recreate a 600-year-old marketplace along Cheonggye Stream this Saturday during its annual Yukuijeon Festival — a celebration named after the "Six Licensed Stores" that held exclusive royal monopolies during the Joseon Dynasty (1392–1910). The 2026 festival will run from 1 to 8 p.m. on Nov. 7 around Jangtonggyo Bridge, bringing together local merchants, food vendors, traditional games and live performances under the theme "Unjong-ga, Street Where People Gather Like Clouds." Unjong-ga was one of Joseon-era Seoul's principal commercial streets, centered around what is now Jongno intersection, where government-authorized merchants and independent traders gathered to sell their goods. The festival takes its name from Yukuijeon, the six major categories of government-authorized shops that once dominated the district's commerce: silk, cotton fabric, hemp fabric, paper, miscellaneous textiles and seafood. item.title: Incheon Int'l Airport uses AI to predict baggage system failures
item.description: Incheon International Airport, Korea’s main international gateway, has begun using artificial intelligence (AI) to spot signs of trouble in its baggage handling system (BHS) before equipment breaks down, its operator said Monday. Incheon International Airport Corp. said its BHS Smart Monitoring System has been running in the baggage handling system at the airport’s Terminal 2 since Oct. 26. BHS is a network of conveyors and sorting machines that moves checked luggage between check-in counters, aircraft and arrival halls. The system tracks key equipment in real time, including baggage sorters, the motors that drive the conveyors and the baggage carousels in arrival halls. Sensors collect data from the equipment, and machine-learning software analyzes it to find parts that are likely to fail. Results are shown on a three-level color scale, with green for normal, yellow for caution and red for danger, along with the likely cause of each problem. Maintenance crews can then replace parts or take other steps before a fault occurs. Under the old approach, crews mostly made repairs after par

item.title: Deoksu Palace brings imperial feasts back to life with AI exhibition
item.description: Visitors to Deoksu Palace will have a chance to become royal chefs, using artificial intelligence (AI) to create elaborate banquet dishes inspired by the dining traditions of the Korean Empire. The Korea Heritage Service's Deoksu Palace Management Office, in collaboration with Davero Art, will open “Imperial Banquet of the Korean Empire, Prepared With AI” on Tuesday at Dondeokjeon Hall in central Seoul, with the exhibition running through March 28, 2027. The interactive exhibition combines historical research into royal Western-style banquets with generative AI, allowing visitors to select ingredients and design their own imperial menus. More than 60 artifacts and exhibition items related to royal banquets will also be displayed, including chandeliers decorated with the imperial plum blossom emblem, iron cooking utensils and matching tableware. At the center of the experience are 30 ingredient models, including lamb, pheasant, salmon, truffles and caviar. item.title: Everland invites visitors to enjoy fall foliage, baby animals, special shows
item.description: Everland, Korea’s largest theme park, said Monday that visitors can enjoy peak fall foliage, newly unveiled baby animals and seasonal shows this month. Autumn leaves across the park are expected to peak this week, according to Samsung C&T’s resort division, which operates the park in Yongin, Gyeonggi Province, about 40 kilometers south of Seoul. Members of Garden Pass, the park’s garden subscription service, can now join a guided program at the Secret Ginkgo Forest near Everland. The company says it is Korea’s largest ginkgo grove, with some 30,000 trees that have grown over more than half a century on about 150,000 square meters of land. Participants can walk the forest with a guide and meditate in hammocks. Visitors can also see the foliage from rides such as Thunder Falls, a rapids ride, and Monimo Rush, which lifts riders 56 meters above the ground. At Panda World, Shubao, a 5-month-old giant panda cub, has been on public display since Oct. 30. item.title: Korean travelers favor nearby Asia as Europe, North America lose ground
item.description: Lee Ji-yeon, an office worker in her 30s, traveled solo to Japan's Kyoto in early October. She had considered destinations such as Canada and Australia, but ultimately opted for a shorter trip closer to home. "It was difficult for me to take a long day off work, and considering the cost of airfare, I thought it would make more sense to take a short trip to a nearby country," she said. A Seoul resident in her 60s surnamed Park is planning a trip to Hong Kong with friends in December. "Long-distance travel has become physically demanding for me, so I ruled out destinations in Europe and North America. Traveling to other Asian countries is more convenient," Park said. Their choices reflect a broader shift in Koreans' overseas travel habits. Japan and China are attracting a growing share of Korean travelers, while Europe and North America are losing ground, according to data released Monday. An analysis by BC Card of Koreans' overseas travel spending found that Asia accounted for 74.3 percent of their overseas travel spending in the first half of this year, from 60.4 percent in the same period

item.description: Kim Se-woong, a former Kakao executive overseeing AI synergy initiatives, has been appointed to lead a government task force developing artificial intelligence (AI) services for the public. According to the Ministry of Science and ICT on Monday, it has appointed Kakao’s former vice president as head of the National AI Service Innovation Task Force. Kim brings extensive experience in AI services, spanning technology development, service commercialization and infrastructure development, as well as organizational management. He founded and ran a tech startup, MightyWorks, in 2009 before joining Kakao, where he held senior roles in AI-related business and technology initiatives. The ministry said his experience in both AI services and organizational management would help the task force establish itself quickly and deliver services at a faster pace. item.title: Korea, Japan seek closer customs cooperation on drugs, counterfeits
item.description: Korea and Japan are seeking to tighten customs cooperation on drug smuggling, counterfeit products and cross-border online shopping, as officials look to protect businesses and strengthen border security. Korea Customs Service Commissioner Lee Jong-wook met with Mitsuhiro Teraoka, director-general of Japan's Customs and Tariff Bureau, in Tokyo last week to discuss three areas of cooperation, the customs agency said Monday. The meeting followed the 34th Korea-Japan Customs Chiefs' Meeting in Seoul in April and was arranged separately to address pressing bilateral issues following Lee's appointment. One priority is protecting Korean and Japanese brands, including K-beauty products, from counterfeit goods. Korea proposed closer enforcement cooperation between the two countries' customs authorities and asked Japan to help Korean companies use its system for requesting customs authorities to block imports and exports of goods suspected of infringing intellectual property rights.
